$comment: Copy deck for the DRIVE-BY bucket: plate-camera matches with NO prior relationship to Ferrario Ford. Not in the DMS, never serviced, never bought here. Voice: DriveOne Red Bull register. Deadpan, cheeky, confident. No exclamation points. No em dashes or en dashes. Never call the DriveOne product a warranty. NEVER claim a relationship: no 'you are a customer', no 'on file', no 'thanks for coming in', no 'we know your car'. The email is an INTRODUCTION from the local Ford store with a real price in it. Never explain how the vehicle was identified and never mention cameras or plates. The odometer is an ESTIMATE (15,000 miles a year of age) and every mileage mention says so and points at checkout to confirm. Sent from the DriveOne Service subdomain as 'Ferrario Ford with DriveOne Service', so Email 1 owns who is writing and why.

campaign.name: An introduction with a price in it: VSC offer to drivers near Ferrario Ford
campaign.audience: Vehicles identified near the dealership with no relationship to Ferrario Ford and no vehicle service contract known to us, deduped against every other Ferrario campaign

smsNote: NO SMS FOR THIS BUCKET. These are plate matches with no relationship to the dealership and no prior express consent of any kind. The TCPA requires prior express written consent for marketing texts; an email list built from plate matches has none, and a STOP-capable text is not consent. The sms array is empty on purpose so workflow 09 has nothing to send even if it is deployed. Do not copy the service drive deck's texts back in.

body: First, who this is. {{dealer_name}} is the Ford dealership at 2472 Corning Rd in Elmira, and we sell vehicle service contracts through DriveOne Service. This email comes from both of us. You have not been in, we are not pretending you have, and it is not the call you keep getting about your car's extended warranty.

The price at the top is for a {{vehicle_year}} {{vehicle_model}} at an estimated {{vehicle_mileage}} miles. We do not have the odometer, so we assumed about fifteen thousand miles a year. At checkout you type in the real number and the price updates before you pay anything.

What it buys is our top plan, Platinum, with a payment plan at zero percent and no credit check. Without it, the next repair that is not routine is priced at whatever it costs. With it, the repair is priced at your deductible. That is the whole decision, and it is yours to make at 11pm in a kitchen if that is when you have four minutes.

body: A {{vehicle_year}} {{vehicle_model}} is a normal car having a normal life, and normal cars eventually produce a bill that is not routine. Alternators. Transmissions. Infotainment units that cost more than your first car. None of them fail on a schedule you get to see coming.
Routine maintenance is not covered by any vehicle service contract, ours included, so we are not going to pretend the oil changes become free.

The bill this is for is the other one. A covered repair, brought to {{dealer_name}}, costs you nothing at all. The only decision is whether to price that now, while the car is healthy, or later, when it is not.

body: You already know what buying coverage usually feels like. Somebody reads a script. Somebody offers to check with a manager. Somebody calls back on a Tuesday.

We took all of that out. You open your quote, you type in your mileage, you pick a plan, you check out. The whole thing is online and it is yours to do at 11pm in a kitchen if that is when you have a spare four minutes.
If you would genuinely like to talk to a human at {{dealer_short}}, our service line is at the bottom of this email and they are good. But you will never need to use it to buy this.

emails.goal: Educate on exclusionary vs listed-component, the real quality differentiator
emails.subject: The good kind of coverage has an ugly name
emails.preheader: Most plans list what is covered. Ours lists what is not. That gap is the whole game.
emails.headline: Platinum. [[Our best.]] Also the only one here.
emails.subhead: We sell one plan in this program and it is the top one. Exclusionary coverage, which is the good kind and has the worst name in the business.
body: A listed component plan names the parts it covers. If your part is not on the list, it is not covered, and the list is always shorter than the car.

An exclusionary plan flips it. It names the short list of things it does not cover, and everything else is in. You are reading a page instead of a phone book, and the burden sits with us rather than with you.
Exclusionary is the coverage level that usually costs extra elsewhere. Here it is the only one we sell, because Platinum is the only plan in this program.

emails.subhead: You have had the call about your vehicle's extended warranty. Possibly during dinner. Possibly twice. You have also seen the ads offering coverage by monthly subscription.
body: Here is the difference, and it is not subtle. Those callers do not know what you drive. The price in this email was built for a {{vehicle_year}} {{vehicle_model}}, and the store it comes from is one you could drive to this afternoon.

The subscription pitch is its own thing. A subscription covers you for as long as you keep paying it, at whatever the price becomes. What we sell is a contract: a term, a mileage allowance and a price, all fixed on the day you buy, transferable if you sell the car, refundable in full for 30 days.

So we are not a call center that bought your number, and we are not an app with a monthly charge. We are a Ford dealership and the service company it chose to work with. Coverage is administered by {{administrator}} and honored at any licensed repair facility they authorize, which makes it a real contract with a real obligor.

body: Coverage gets sold on the catastrophic repair. In practice, the parts people use most are the small ones, and they work anywhere in the country rather than only in our zip code.
A tow on a Sunday night. A rental car while yours sits on a lift for three days. A sensor you had never heard of, which turns out to be essential.
None of that makes for dramatic advertising. All of it makes for a better Tuesday.

emails.subhead: We have avoided fake deadlines for eight emails. Here is the real one.
body: Vehicle service contracts are underwritten against mileage and model year. Every plan has a ceiling, and we priced your {{vehicle_year}} {{vehicle_model}} at an estimated {{vehicle_mileage}} miles. If the real number is lower, good news at checkout. If it is higher, the window is narrower than this email suggests.

Nothing expires this Friday. No countdown clock is running. But coverage is additive: the term and the miles start the day you buy and get added to wherever the car is then. Every month you wait is a month of protection you are not holding, on a car that is quietly getting older.
Coverage cannot be bought retroactively. That is the entire reason this campaign exists.
